Industry News: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Nvidia-Megaspeed saga has drawn attention to a significant gap in U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that but while this long-overdue action can help U.S.
  • Sources indicate that the Trump administration wants the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nvidia-Megaspeed saga has drawn attention to a significant gap in U.S. export controls: Chinese companies remotely accessing AI chips located outside of China. On Monday, largely in response to the scandal, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a rule closing this loophole.

Recent findings suggest that but while this long-overdue action can help U.S. AI labs widen the gap between their models and those of their Chinese competitors, there’s still a paradox at the heart of Washington’s AI strategy: the U.S. infrastructure spreading around the world is helping Chinese models gain traction.

Sources indicate that the Trump administration wants the U.S. to dominate AI from chips to models. Key to the president’s vision is exporting high-end, U.S.-designed chips to countries around the world. Increasingly, these chips—designed by companies like Nvidia—are being deployed in data centers in Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia.

But U.S. leadership in compute infrastructure doesn’t just help U.S. AI model developers. It helps their Chinese competitors too.

Today, U.S.-owned data centers filled with U.S. chips still rent capacity out to inference providers, which use that capability to serve Chinese large language models (LLMs) to global owners.

Sources indicate that chinese models are running on U.S. chips, and the U.S. AI infrastructure build-out is counterintuitively helping Chinese model developers compete. This poses a problem for U.S. AI preeminence, which will need global consumers and enterprises to choose U.S.-developed LLMs over Chinese ones.

The contradiction at the heart of the Trump administration’s dreams of AI dominance is that success at one layer of the stack is undermining its goals at another.

Industry observers note that when people hear that Chinese models are gaining customers, they generally assume that those models are running on Chinese chips. While that’s increasingly the case within China, the truth is that China cannot produce enough advanced AI chips to satisfy its own companies, let alone meet overseas demand.

Meanwhile, America’s grip on AI infrastructure is formidable. U.S. companies—Nvidia, Google, AMD, and Amazon—design nearly all deployed data-center AI chips. In cloud services, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google together control more than half of the market, with a growing cohort of U.S. “neoclouds” further extending that lead.

Yet the same infrastructure that secures America’s advantage in chips and cloud services gives Chinese AI models a platform to spread. Nvidia itself provides resources to help companies deploy open models—including several Chinese models—on its hardware. U.S.-based model inference providers such as Together AI, Baseten, and Fireworks serve Chinese models to customers on infrastructure powered by U.S. chips. For example, DeepSeek’s latest model is being offered by at least 16 inference providers headquartered outside China, including Amazon Bedrock.

Industry observers note that when U.S. infrastructure is used to serve Chinese LLMs, it accelerates those models’ global adoption, which in turn benefits China’s soft power and generates revenue for its AI labs. Beijing’s stated ambition is to be the leading provider of transformative AI capabilities, especially in the Global South. Wider adoption of Chinese LLMs advances that objective.

Chinese LLM deployments also generate direct revenue for Chinese model developers. For example, Moonshot AI requires companies that serve its successful Kimi K3 model and exceed $20 million in annual sales to negotiate a revenue-sharing license; Moonshot has reportedly asked Microsoft, Amazon, and Google for 30% of their Kimi K3 revenue.

It has been revealed that today, who benefits from U.S. computing infrastructure depends on whether it serves proprietary or open-weight models. On one side are proprietary LLMs such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s GPT. Infrastructure serving proprietary models almost exclusively benefits American developers, because they make the best ones. On the other side are open-weight LLMs, which companies can customize for specialized tasks and run locally. Infrastructure serving open-weight LLMs benefits Chinese developers: customers tend to choose the best available models, and in the open-weight market, those are Chinese.

The Trump administration, however, should not go so far as to ban U.S. cloud providers from allowing non-Chinese companies to serve Chinese LLMs. Doing so would incur too high a cost—unjustifiably hindering companies in the United States and allied countries seeking to adopt AI—while failing to deliver sufficient national security benefits. It could also invite Chinese retaliation.

In a recent development, instead, the United States should compete. Some U.S. companies like Meta and Thinking Machines are already developing open-weight models. If they become more cost-efficient than their Chinese competitors, more U.S. computing infrastructure would serve U.S. models. That shift could limit both the revenue Chinese developers earn from overseas deployments and the soft power China gains from its models’ global reach.

The Trump administration is therefore correct to encourage the development of competitive U.S. open-weight models. It should identify government uses well-suited to open-weight models and direct federal procurement toward American open-weight models for those uses. Finally, as stronger AI regulation becomes necessary, the administration should design those rules carefully to avoid stifling U.S. open-weight model development.

It has been revealed that washington can’t assume that exporting U.S. infrastructure will automatically lead to the export of U.S. models. If it wants to succeed on both fronts, it needs a deliberate strategy for open-weight models.

  • Sources indicate that XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median.
  • XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

XRP stands out as the cryptocurrency with the most alarming volatility warning among major digital assets, according to recent Coinbase data. The options market indicates that traders are now preparing for price swings that could be nearly double XRP's historical seven-day price move.

Sources indicate that XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median. This figure far exceeds similar metrics for major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH) and Solana (SOL).

XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility. Solana reveals the lowest premium among these four cryptocurrencies, Coinbase remarked.

Sources indicate that as the chart below indicates, the options-implied seven-day price move for XRP is around 9.6%, according to Glassnode and Coinbase data as of Nov. 17. This compares to its historical median absolute price move of about 4.9%.

Basically, this means that the options market is signaling a price swing nearly twice as large as XRP's typical seven-day price movement.

It has been revealed that interestingly, Solana's implied price move is also close to 9.5%, almost the same as XRP's. Yet its historical median weekly price move is much higher at about 6.5%.

The key here is that although both cryptocurrencies exhibit similarly large potential price moves, the magnitude of the expected volatility surprise is significantly greater for XRP relative to its usual trading range.

For comparison, Bitcoin shows an options-implied seven-day move of about 6%, versus its historical median of about 3.5%. For Ethereum, these numbers are about 8% and 5.1%, respectively.

Sources indicate that obviously, this latest figure doesn't necessarily imply that XRP is going to crash. It's a sign that options traders expect a major price move regardless of its direction.

Implied volatility is a forward-looking measure. It's based on options prices. The higher the implied volatility, the more traders pay for exposure to potential price movements or protection against them.

The chart from Coinbase is based on a one-standard-deviation estimate. It's derived by converting annualized at-the-money implied volatility into a seven-day timeframe.

Recent findings suggest that for XRP, the roughly 9.6% implied move represents a statistical range. It's not a guaranteed price target. A one-standard-deviation range suggests about a 68% chance of the price staying within this range under typical modeling assumptions.

Thus, the latest figure of 1.94x implies that XRP's volatility premium remains high despite a slight decrease from the previous reading.

It has been revealed that from XRP traders' perspective, this can be a very challenging market environment. For traders using leverage, there could be a high risk of liquidation due to potentially sharp price moves.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3.
  • The most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made.
  • Industry observers note that on November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

The most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

Industry observers note that on November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

Sources indicate that it also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

It has been revealed that early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

Industry observers note that the staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

Industry observers note that the second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

According to recent reports, legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself indicates the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the complications presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

According to recent reports, in practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

Industry observers note that the framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

It has been revealed that that sequence matters. The interpretation indicates what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

According to recent reports, for now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

Sources indicate that U.S. investors are facing a meltdown in tech stocks and the possible end of the AI boom, but the bubble has already popped in China, where an even worse market crash threatens the economy and President Xi Jinping, according to Yardeni Research.

China’s tech-heavy STAR 50 index has tumbled 44% from its high this summer, while the Nasdaq is down 18% from its record—even after U.S. stocks suffered their worst week since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

In a recent development, that’s thrown a wrench into Xi’s plans for the economy, Yardeni said in a note earlier this month. While the Chinese leader was riding high as host to global leaders this week, the market’s downturn jeopardizes his blueprint to turn China’s savers into stock investors who can finance the AI buildout and de-emphasize the property market.

Recent findings suggest that real estate accounts for roughly 70% of household wealth in China and was traditionally a place to stash savings. But the housing crash has weighed on consumer demand, even producing intermittent deflation. Business investment is also falling, with October data showing property investment sank nearly 22%.

With the domestic market still weak, Beijing has instead relied on a flood of cheap exports to keep the economy growing while also deploying the “national team” of state-backed banks to pump money into the stock market.

But according to Yardeni, Chinese stocks collapsed this year due in part to cutthroat competition, heavier tax burdens, higher energy costs, tariffs, and the risk that China’s trading partners will block exports being sold at ultra-low prices.

According to recent reports, “To keep AI funding flowing, Xi needs a buoyant stock market,” the note said. “Otherwise, AI risks being folded into the state-owned enterprise (SOE) universe that his team has pledged to shrink since 2013, further crowding out the private sector.”.

Industry observers note that retail investors are also skittish about Chinese stocks after Xi’s government cracked down on the tech sector in 2020. The market’s reputation as a rigged casino that favors politically connected insiders doesn’t help either. In fact, the Shanghai Composite remains well below its October 2007 peak despite China’s GDP exploding nearly sixfold.

Many households now have “financial PTSD” after repeated stock busts, including a crash in the summer of 2015 that required an aggressive national team rescue, Yardeni added.

To be sure, China remains a leader in AI, and mom-and-pop investors still drive most of the trade, even as they treat the market more like high-stakes gambling than a place to grow retirement savings.

In a recent development, “Yet this is a moment of real danger for Xi. A bursting AI bubble would not merely erase wealth or dent China’s technological prestige. It would weaken Beijing’s attempt to replace a broken property model with a stock-market-led one,” Yardeni warned.

“China can build world-class AI models, train engineers, and spend billions on chips. But if its households still view Shanghai as a casino with odds set by the Politburo, Xi’s dream of creating a Chinese version of Wall Street may remain just that: a dream.”.

Underscoring its importance to Beijing, Premier Li Qiang told a State Council executive meeting earlier this month that stabilizing capital markets was the top priority for the rest of the year.

It followed securities regulators sharply easing requirements for manufacturer buybacks that help lift stock prices and discouraging IPOs and large share sales to prevent stock dilution that triggers selloffs.

But the spy scandal that dethroned Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia represents a newly introduced risk to China’s AI ambitions. Backlash over the advanced U.S. chips and computing capacity that China had access to has spurred the Trump administration to impose new technology curbs.

“By targeting both indirect chip shipments to China and its access to overseas computing power, the new controls threaten to slow the catch-up of China’s leading AI models and to slow China’s AI rollout,” analysts at Capital Economics wrote on Tuesday.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.
  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

In a recent development, zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles mentioned. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

Industry observers note that retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “notable step toward undersea superiority.”.

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson stated in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

Next year, Zeno Power intends to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

In a recent development, the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The tech giant is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

“A modest pullback in the data center buildout could give cash flows time to catch up, easing inflation pressures and making the investment boom more sustainable,” he argued.

Slower prices could prevent additional rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, which has grown more hawkish as policymakers become impatient with inflation exceeding their 2% target for over five years.

Although Wall Street sees more tightening in the coming months, some analysts also anticipate rate cuts later in 2027 as inflation cools. But that assumes the Iran war will be over some time next year.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.
  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with substantial financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with substantial financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The organization started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Sources indicate that beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old manufacturer was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the manufacturer to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

It has been revealed that what’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The firm states revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero.

The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing.

Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a latest technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns.

OpenAI’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users.

By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. Already, Anthropic notes 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1, the manufacturer says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record.

Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it notes it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology.

Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets:.

Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn-led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the tech giant at $965 billion.

Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google, Amazon, Spark Capital, Menlo Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow.

The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension.

The opportunity the firm describes extends far beyond coding and software. It indicates its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services.

That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses.

Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption.

Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company claims it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science. Anthropic points to its launch of Mythos as an example of that balance.

As Anthropic debuts tomorrow, I’ll be watching how well it balances AI’s promise with the risks its own filing lays out.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no upcoming mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain claims nothing moves unless it passes.

Sources indicate that if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's latest private AI app, ZetaLabs, launches alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a newly introduced whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

Recent findings suggest that the snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Industry observers note that holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

In a recent development, on Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

In a recent development, that sequence is the strongest holder protection in the blueprint, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain states it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

According to recent reports, the biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange people depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

According to recent reports, the vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Sources indicate that taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The network itself was barely 1 year old, and its future raised more questions than answers.
  • In 2010, the revolution began: 10,000 BTC was used to buy two pizzas, one of the first uses of the digital asset in exchange for a commodity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On this day, 17 years ago, Satoshi Nakamoto opened an account on BitcoinTalk, the place that would become the home of early Bitcoin enthusiasts and then turn into a public forum for crypto in general, until social media platforms took over the internet.

The network itself was barely 1 year old, and its future raised more questions than answers. Satoshi Nakamoto welcomed customers on the forum and invited any questions people had regarding the cryptocurrency.

In 2010, the revolution began: 10,000 BTC was used to buy two pizzas, one of the first uses of the digital asset in exchange for a commodity. In May, Laszlo Hanyecz probably had the most expensive pizza dinner in history, considering how much BTC rallied after that. By December, Satoshi made their final BitcoinTalk post and announced their farewell.

According to recent reports, the 2011-2014 period turned out to be the foundation for the network as a whole. Bitcoin became an open-source project maintained by others. The first halving happened in November 2012 and reduced the block issuance from 50 to 25 BTC per block.

The first-ever exchange implosion, Mt.Gox in 2014, raised serious questions about the security and stability of centralized exchanges, an issue we haven't solved 17 years later.

Sources indicate that 2017-2021 were the years when the industry truly blossomed. We had our first bull run on Bitcoin, which pushed the price above expected levels, to almost $20,000 in December 2017, along with the first altcoin bull run and the birth of new technologies like smart contracts, NFTs and many more. The next cycle took Bitcoin to around $69,000 in November 2021.

However, with the growth of the industry, multiple conflicts arose around safety, integrity and usage. The first country in the world to adopt Bitcoin was El Salvador, which implemented the digital currency as a true means of payment, in addition to accumulating it in its treasury.

Recent findings suggest that 2022 was the pivotal year, marked by the FTX and Terra crashes that changed how investors treat markets in general. FTX wasn't just an exchange: it was the backbone of the cryptocurrency market in those years. It aimed to rival Binance and become the bridge between institutional investors and crypto.

However, poor risk management, complications with fund allocation and many other factors caused an implosion that ended the bull run.

Industry observers note that in 2024, Wall Street arrived in crypto with ETFs, ETPs, perpetual futures and a regulatory framework. The digital assets industry became a part of a larger market. Whether that is good or bad is a question to consider, but one thing is clear: Bitcoin has come a very long way since 2010 and is evolving to this day.

Industry observers note that the next step is the arrival of AI and rising cybersecurity risks, which go toe-to-toe with the quantum danger. How the first cryptocurrency handles them is a question that directly affects its future.

Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious strategy to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.
  • In a recent development, editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.

In a recent development, editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid promptly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Industry observers note that underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he mentioned.

According to recent reports, he founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

It has been revealed that nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

Sources indicate that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he noted. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

Sources indicate that after graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk firm developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

According to recent reports, “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd mentioned. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In a recent development, in 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in latest natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who stated the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

Recent findings suggest that in launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd mentioned, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion manufacturer Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

According to recent reports, A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

Sources indicate that while the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

According to recent reports, endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

According to recent reports, the company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

Recent findings suggest that “This was always the end goal,” Redd stated. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

Major crypto exchange Coinbase shared the options-implied seven-day ratios for major cryptocurrencies, highlighting that options traders might be preparing for an unusually large price move for XRP.

In an X post, Coinbase Markets shared the outcome of dividing the options-implied 7-day move by the median 7-day move for XRP, Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana.

Options-implied 7d move, divided by each asset's own median 7d move: $XRP 1.94× $BTC 1.69× $ETH 1.56× $SOL 1.46× $XRP is priced furthest above its own history, $SOL the least. Which one is asking for more than its own history delivered? https://t.co/WgWbqjcgwI.

In a recent development, this suggests how much movement options markets are pricing in relative to each asset's own historical behavior. However, it does not compare their expected dollar or percentage moves directly.

According to the figures shared by Coinbase, XRP's options-implied seven-day move stands at 1.94 times its own historical median seven-day move. Bitcoin follows at 1.69 times, while Ethereum records 1.56 times and Solana comes in at 1.46 times.

XRP, therefore has the highest relative reading among the four assets, suggesting options traders are pricing in a more pronounced move than the token has typically delivered over a comparable period.

At the time of writing, XRP was down 1.93% in the last 24 hours to $0.98 amid the continued profit-taking in the market. XRP briefly reached $1 on November 18, 2026, but fell afterwards as traders took profits. XRP is down 21.57% so far in November, but its history says more than its current price action does.

It has been revealed that XRP’s average November gain is skewed upward by massive outlier rallies—specifically +550% in 2013 and +282% in 2024. Its median November return is about -10%, meaning it has closed lower in most cycles in history. XRP dropped roughly 23.42% in November 2019 and lost 12.18% in November 2025 (opening at around $2.51 and closing at around $2.20).

A weak November doesn’t always mean a weak December: for instance, after falling 9.1% in November 2015, XRP jumped 46.8% in December 2015.

In the near term, XRP’s price recovery will target $1 before moving to the $1.24–$1.26 range. Alternatively, if the price falls further, it is likely to find support at $0.89.

Ahmed Barakat is a journalist and copywriter based in Georgia with a growing focus on blockchain technology, DeFi, AI, privacy, digital assets, and fintech innovation.

Industry observers note that the CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price has fallen below $62,000 for the first time since early July, extending a brutal November selloff as institutional investors pull billions from the market. BTC touched $61,270 just now, before recovering slightly to trade around $61,700.

Bitcoin price has now lost more than 10% over seven days, with selling pressure spreading across equities, precious metals and other risk assets. Yesterday’s $582.2 million outflow from US spot Bitcoin ETFs added another blow, bringing November withdrawals close to $3.5 billion.

Industry observers note that blackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541.1 million of Thursday’s withdrawals, its largest single-day outflow since launching. The same session saw $727 million in crypto liquidations, with bullish traders absorbing most of the damage.

Institutional demand is weakening, leveraged buyers are being forced out, and the Federal Reserve’s increasingly hawkish outlook is making speculative assets less attractive.

Bitcoin is now approaching $60,000, a level that could determine if the correction finds a floor or develops into something uglier.

Recent findings suggest that the ETF withdrawals are arguably the biggest concern for Bitcoin holders right now. Spot Bitcoin ETFs became an important source of institutional demand after launching in January 2024. Their buying helped absorb available supply and gave traditional investors a regulated route into the market.

Recent findings suggest that that demand is now moving in the opposite direction. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost more than $1.1 billion this week alone. November’s cumulative withdrawals have approached $3.5 billion.

The pressure extends beyond ETFs. Rising Treasury yields and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase in December have encouraged investors to reduce exposure to assets that offer no regular income.

Meanwhile, derivatives traders are taking heavy losses. CoinGlass data showed more than $700 million in liquidations across crypto markets over 24 hours. Long positions accounted for 86% of the total.

Bitcoin itself recorded nearly $202 million in liquidations, with bullish traders suffering the majority of forced closures.

Recent findings suggest that this creates a difficult environment for buyers. Falling prices trigger liquidations, which create additional selling pressure and push prices lower. The reduction in open interest also suggests excessive leverage is being flushed from the market.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

In a recent development, the immediate battle is around $60,000. Bitcoin needs to reclaim $62,000 and establish support above it before bulls can confidently argue that the latest breakdown was temporary.

There are three possible scenarios:.

Scenario 1: Bitcoin loses $60K and heads toward $58K or $53K.

This is the bearish outcome. A decisive break below $60,000 could trigger another wave of stop-loss orders and leveraged liquidations.

The next downside area sits around $58,000, while more aggressive technical projections point toward $53,700.

According to recent reports, the daily chart offers little encouragement for bulls. Bitcoin trades below its major moving averages, while bearish momentum continues to dominate. A sustained recovery in ETF flows would become increasingly key to prevent further deterioration.

Scenario 2: Bitcoin stabilizes between $60K and $62K.

This would give buyers time to absorb available supply without immediately reversing the entire November decline.

The liquidation wave has already removed considerable leverage from the market. If ETF withdrawals begin slowing, Bitcoin could establish a trading range before attempting another recovery.

But sideways trading alone would not confirm a bottom. Buyers need to demonstrate that they can defend support through multiple sessions.

Scenario 3: Bitcoin reclaims $62K and releases a relief rally.

A recovery above $62,000 would provide the first meaningful sign that sellers are losing control. A move toward $65,000 would then become possible, followed by resistance around $68,000.

Consistent ETF inflows, improving market sentiment, and a weaker dollar would strengthen this scenario. Without those developments, any rebound risks becoming another opportunity for sellers to exit.

Industry observers note that for existing holders, the decision depends heavily on their entry price, investment horizon, and exposure. Long-term holders who bought substantially below current prices have more room to withstand volatility. Selling simply because Bitcoin crossed a psychological threshold risks locking in profits or losses without knowing whether the broader investment thesis has changed.

However, investors holding leveraged positions face a different problem. Falling prices can trigger forced liquidations regardless of their long-term convictions. Reducing leverage and protecting available capital should take priority over waiting for a rebound.

It has been revealed that for buyers, the temptation to buy the dip is understandable. Bitcoin is considerably cheaper than it was just weeks ago, but cheaper does not automatically mean undervalued.

Buying in stages rather than committing an entire allocation around $61,000 offers more flexibility if the market tests $58,000 or even $53,700.

In a recent development, bitcoin price remains vulnerable to another leg down. The $60,000 level is no longer just a psychological milestone. It is where the next major battle between buyers and sellers.

So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1392 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.
  • Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn.
  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the firm’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Massive Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the firm’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman confirmed the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft notes the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

Recent findings suggest that all of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in fresh hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a firm right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

Industry observers note that there is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

Recent findings suggest that but it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one manufacturer.

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more crucial than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI firm today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Sources indicate that hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software organization.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a organization.

Industry observers note that software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue promptly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

Sources indicate that the bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

Industry observers note that one venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

Industry observers note that 1) Think VERY massive, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a tech giant that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

Sources indicate that there are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

In a recent development, whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Substantial Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a fresh role, a firm of their own or a year with their family.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shares of Anthropic closed up 17% in first-day trading Thursday amid an otherwise down day for the broader market.

Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday evening, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing.

According to recent reports, the offering promised to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

It has been revealed that for the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, including 23.6 million from selling shareholders, up from it’s earlier plan to sell just over 800 million shares. At that upgraded size, the offering is bringing in around $80 billion for the company.

Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

Put together, the IPO and private placement total around $106 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX, by comparison, raised $86 billion in its June offering.

The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books.

For the first nine months of the year, the tech giant had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago.

Anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.

As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

Industry News: webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B.
  • A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500.
  • webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

The card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It says TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight people want to hear.

In a recent development, on MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

In a recent development, here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

Recent findings suggest that none of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

It has been revealed that read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Recent findings suggest that against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card highlights the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a big generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 upcoming tokens and a 40,960-token context.

It has been revealed that anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card notes all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

Recent findings suggest that the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Industry observers note that overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

Sources indicate that the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

In a recent development, on Nov. 18, Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) added the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid to its list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms. The listing covers the web interface of the Hyperliquid trading terminal at app.hyperliquid.xyz/trade. The HYPE token dropped to around $65.50 on the evening of Nov. 18, and it recovered to $68.79 by midday Nov. 19, according to TradingView data.

According to recent reports, according to the entry, the organization claims to provide digital asset trading services on the website, and it has no address on record. Hyperliquid is not licensed by the SFC, and it is suspected of operating a virtual asset trading platform in Hong Kong or actively promoting its services to the public, the regulator noted.

In an accompanying warning, the SFC reminded investors that such platforms often lure users with "incredible investment opportunities." The SFC also reminded investors that clients of unlicensed platforms have no legal protection if a platform is hacked or misappropriates their assets.

According to recent reports, on the same day, the Hyperliquid Policy Center (HPC) sent a letter to the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority with seven recommendations on the country's upcoming crypto rules. "Regulatory obligations belong with persons who have unilateral control over a function that is a regulated activity," the group wrote.

On Nov. 16, two days before the SFC added Hyperliquid to the list, Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan spoke at the Bloomberg Global Regulatory Forum. "Before the end of this year, we will introduce a bill to complete the regulatory perimeter," Chan said.

It has been revealed that according to Chan, the bill will cover crypto dealers, custodians, advisers and asset managers. "Decentralisation does not mean less accountability," he said.

In April, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority licensed HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial as the first stablecoin issuers in the city, out of 36 applicants in the first round.

Breaking: Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it
